explanation: A nimble person moves quickly and lightly, which is what "agile" names. "Graceful" reports how pleasing the movement is to watch, and a slow movement can be graceful; "sturdy" reports what the body can take rather than how it moves; and "upright" reports how a person holds himself when he is standing still. All four could be said of the same dancer.

To boast is to speak of one's own doings as finer than they are, which is what "brag" names. "Insist" presses a point without praising anybody; "complain" reports what is wrong rather than what is admirable; and "announce" makes a thing publicly known and says nothing about the worth of the speaker. All four are ways of speaking up in company.

To forbid a practice is to rule that it may not go on, which is what "outlaw" names. "Enforce" is what a body does with a rule it has already made; "delay" puts the practice off for a while and leaves it allowed; and "review" only looks at it again. All four are things a town council can do about the same practice.

Sparse growth has wide gaps in it, so "thinly scattered" is the match. "Crowded together" is the same measure run the other way; "newly planted" reports when the growth went in rather than how much of it there is; and "evenly trimmed" reports that it has been cut to one height, which a thin patch and a thick patch can both be. All four describe a strip of grass along a path.

To baffle someone is to leave him unable to make sense of a thing, which is what "puzzle" names. "Irritate" reports a temper rather than an understanding; "persuade" moves his opinion, which requires that he followed the argument; and "discourage" takes away his willingness to go on, which is a matter of spirit rather than of sense. All four are things a hard problem can do to the person working on it.

An obstinate person will not be moved off the position he has taken, which is what "unyielding" names. "Unhurried" fixes his pace; "unreliable" whether he can be counted on to do what he said; and "unconcerned" whether he cares how the matter comes out. All four might be said of the same man across one afternoon of bargaining.

A vigilant person keeps a steady lookout for whatever may go wrong, which is what "watchful" names. "Patient" reports how long he will wait without complaint; "hopeful" what he expects to come of the waiting; and "apprehensive" how the waiting feels to him. All four describe someone sitting up through the night beside a sick animal, and only one of them concerns what his eyes are doing.

A lenient judge gives less punishment than he might have given, which is what "merciful" names. "Formal" reports the manner he keeps in court; "hesitant" that he has trouble reaching a decision at all; and "thorough" how completely he went through the evidence — a judge can be thorough and then hand down the heaviest sentence available. All four are things said of the same magistrate.

To diminish is to grow steadily less, which is what "dwindle" names. "Stabilize" settles at one level and stops moving; "fluctuate" goes up as often as down and ends nowhere in particular; and "linger" stays on without getting any smaller. All four say what a quantity does as time passes.

An arduous task calls for hard and sustained effort, which is what "demanding" names. "Tedious" reports dullness, and a dull job may cost no effort at all; "hazardous" reports danger, and a dangerous job may be over in a minute; and "unfamiliar" reports only that the work has not been done before. All four describe a job of work.

Something superfluous is more than the occasion requires, so "unnecessary" is the match. "Unfinished" says the thing stops short, which is the opposite complaint; "unexplained" says no reason was given for it; and "uncorroborated" says nothing else on the page backs it up. All four are complaints an editor might write in the margin beside one paragraph.

A parsimonious person parts with money grudgingly even when he has it, so "unwilling to spend" is the match. "Unable to save" is the same subject turned over: it describes someone whose money goes rather than stays; "openhanded with friends" hands it to other people; and "quick to borrow" takes theirs. All four describe how a person stands toward his own money.

An indolent worker will not put himself out, which is what "lazy" names. "Careless" does the work but without attending to it; "clumsy" reports a want of skill in the hands rather than a want of will; and "timid" reports a want of nerve. All four are complaints a foreman might make about the same apprentice.

prompt: The trail map shows a footbridge over the creek, but the bridge washed out two winters ago and the ranger station has not put out a new printing since, so the map is -------.
explanation: The map still shows a bridge that has not stood for two years, and the sentence says outright that no newer printing exists, so what is wrong with it is its age: it is "outdated." "Illegible" would concern how clearly the sheet is printed, and the sentence mentions the printing only to date it; "unofficial" would concern who issued it, and a ranger station is exactly the body that would; and "crowded" would concern how much is packed onto the sheet, which nothing here measures.

prompt: Adaeze read the assembly manual twice before she opened the box, laid all twenty-nine parts out on the floor in the order the diagram gave them, and had the shelf standing in forty minutes; her approach was -------.
explanation: Reading the instructions first and laying the parts out in the given order is working to a plan step by step, which is what "methodical" names. "Improvised" would mean she made the method up as she went, and she had it from the manual; "inspired" would credit some idea of her own, and every step she takes comes from the diagram; and "fortunate" would credit luck, which nothing in a sequence she arranged beforehand is doing.

prompt: The greenhouse was built against the north wall of the warehouse, and the plants on the back bench, the one farthest from the glass, have not put out a new leaf since March, though they are watered and fed on the same schedule as the benches that are thriving; what that bench lacks is -------.
explanation: The failing bench stands farthest from the glass in a house that faces a wall, and the sentence grants it the same watering and feeding as the benches that are doing well, so the one thing left in short supply is "light." "Water" and "fertilizer" are each refused by that clause about the shared schedule; and "space" would show itself as crowding, which would need a count of plants, and the sentence counts none.

prompt: The label beside the painting gives the artist's name, the year, and the medium, and says nothing about the scene, the sitter, or how the picture came to the museum; to a visitor who wants to know what he is looking at, the label is -------.
explanation: The visitor's question is what the picture shows, and all three things the label supplies are facts about the object rather than about the scene, so for his purpose it is "unhelpful." "Inaccurate" would mean the name, the year, or the medium is wrong, and nothing gives a reason to think so; "ornate" would describe how the label is decorated and "faded" the state of its ink, while the sentence describes only what is written on it.

prompt: The committee's minutes are ------- about who proposed the motion and ------- about who opposed it: three names are set down at the head of the entry, and the rest of it says only that there was discussion.
explanation: Three names at the head of the entry answer the first question exactly — "precise" — and an entry that says only that there was discussion answers the second not at all, which is "silent." "Brief . . . thorough" has the halves the wrong way round, since it is the part about the opposition that is short; "cautious . . . admiring" reports an attitude toward the members, and three names and the word discussion express none; and "formal . . . lengthy" breaks on the second blank, because the part of the entry covering the opposition is the shortest thing in it.

prompt: For thirty years the ferry crossed whenever the tide allowed and so never twice at the same hour, and in all that time it failed to cross only once; the service was dependable but -------.
explanation: A boat that goes by the tide leaves at a different hour every day, and "never twice at the same hour" is exactly what "irregular" names, while "dependable" is already granted by the single failure in thirty years. "Expensive" would report the fare and "cramped" the room aboard, neither of which the sentence measures; and "slow" would report how long the crossing takes, which is never given.

prompt: The new bylaw forbids posters on the lampposts and says nothing about the fence along the empty lot, the bus shelter, or the blank side wall of the library, so as a rule against flyposting its coverage is -------.
explanation: One surface named and three of the obvious ones left out is a rule that reaches some of its subject and not the rest, which is "partial." "Illegal" would mean the town had no power to pass it, a question the sentence never raises; "temporary" would need an expiry date, and none is given; and "symbolic" would mean the bylaw was meant to express disapproval rather than to work, and the lampposts it does name are covered in earnest.

prompt: The census of the island counted every occupied house, but it was taken in February, when half the summer cottages stand empty and the families who own them are counted in the cities instead; the figure it produced is accurate for winter and ------- for August.
explanation: In August those families are on the island and the February count has them somewhere else, so the same figure, offered as an August population, points a reader wrong: it is "misleading." "Identical" is what the sentence is built to refuse, since its whole subject is the difference between the two seasons; "unavailable" would mean no August figure could be had, while the figure exists and is simply the winter one; and "generous" would have the count running high, and leaving out half the cottages makes it run low.

prompt: Kwan has kept the shop's books in pencil since 1978, and when a figure changes he erases it and writes the new one in the same square; the books show what every figure is, but not what it -------.
explanation: Erasing puts the new figure in the square where the old one stood, so the page keeps the present value and destroys the earlier one: what is lost is the figure it "replaced." "Cost" would ask about an expense, and a figure in a ledger may as easily be a count or a balance as a price; "means" would ask what the entry stands for, which the column heading tells a reader; and "totals" would ask for a sum, and erasing one square stops nobody from adding the column up.

prompt: Every edition of the atlas printed after 1931 took its coastline from the edition before it, and the 1931 survey was flown in a single afternoon of poor visibility; sixty years of maps are therefore no more accurate than their -------.
explanation: Each edition copies the coastline from the one before, so the whole series carries forward whatever that single 1931 flight got wrong, and what limits every one of them is that "source." "Scale" concerns how much ground an inch stands for, and a coarse scale can still be honest; "printing" concerns how cleanly the plates were struck; and "binding" concerns how the volume is held together — a map can be faultless in all three and still draw the shoreline in the wrong place.

prompt: The prize goes each year to the best first novel written in the county, and in four of the last six years exactly one first novel was written in the county; what a winner's name really records is less the merit of the book than the ------- of the field.
explanation: In four years of the six the field held one book, so winning meant being the only entrant, and what the name on the prize records is how few writers stood against it: the "size" of the field. "Age" would concern how long the field has existed or how old its writers are, and neither is counted; "ambition" would concern what those writers were attempting, and not one book is described; and "generosity" would attach to whoever endowed the prize rather than to the field competing for it.

prompt: The treaty fixes the boundary 'at the river,' and the river has since moved nine hundred yards west of where it ran on the day the treaty was signed; the clause drafted to put the question beyond argument has turned out to be the ------- of the dispute.
explanation: The quarrel exists because the clause fixed the boundary to a thing that moves, so the clause is where the trouble begins: its "origin." "Resolution" is what the clause was drafted to be and what the sentence says it failed to be; "record" would make it a report of a dispute that started somewhere else, and nothing else in the sentence starts one; and "exception" would set it aside from some general rule, and the treaty is given no such rule for it to stand outside of.
